subject: biology
title: Nucleic acids and proteins
summary: How nucleotides build DNA and RNA, how amino acids join to make polypeptides, and how the genetic code links the two.
body:
Every living cell runs on two families of large molecules: nucleic acids, which store and carry instructions, and proteins, which carry those instructions out as enzymes, hormones, channels and structural fibres. Understanding how each is built, and how the genetic code links a sequence of DNA bases to a sequence of amino acids, is the foundation for everything else in Unit 3, from gene expression to genetic engineering.

## Key ideas

### Nucleotides: the building blocks of nucleic acids

**Nucleic acids** are polymers that store or transmit genetic information. The two types are **DNA** (deoxyribonucleic acid) and **RNA** (ribonucleic acid). Both are made of monomers called **nucleotides**.

Each nucleotide has three parts:

- a **phosphate group**
- a five-carbon (**pentose**) sugar: **deoxyribose** in DNA, **ribose** in RNA (ribose has one more oxygen atom, an OH group on carbon 2)
- a **nitrogenous base**

There are five bases. **Adenine (A)** and **guanine (G)** are **purines**, with a double-ring structure. **Cytosine (C)**, **thymine (T)** and **uracil (U)** are **pyrimidines**, with a single ring. DNA uses A, T, G and C. RNA uses A, U, G and C, so uracil replaces thymine.

The carbons in the sugar are numbered 1′ to 5′. The base attaches to the 1′ carbon and the phosphate attaches to the 5′ carbon. This numbering matters because it gives each strand a direction.

### Condensation polymerisation

**Condensation polymerisation** is the joining of many monomers into a polymer, where each new bond releases one molecule of water. It is how both nucleic acids and proteins are built.

In a nucleic acid, the phosphate of one nucleotide bonds to the 3′ carbon of the sugar of the previous nucleotide. This link is a **phosphodiester bond**. Repeating this produces a **sugar-phosphate backbone** with the bases sticking out to the side. One end of the strand has a free phosphate on a 5′ carbon (the **5′ end**) and the other has a free OH on a 3′ carbon (the **3′ end**). New nucleotides are always added to the 3′ end, so strands are built in the 5′ → 3′ direction.

The reverse reaction, which breaks a polymer apart by adding water, is called **hydrolysis**.

### DNA structure

DNA is a **double helix**: two strands wound around each other. Key features:

- **Complementary base pairing**: A always pairs with T, and G always pairs with C. A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, which keeps the helix the same width all along.
- The bases are held together by **hydrogen bonds**: two between A and T, three between G and C. Hydrogen bonds are weak individually, so the strands can be separated for copying and transcription, but together they hold the molecule stable.
- The two strands are **antiparallel**: one runs 5′ → 3′ and the other runs 3′ → 5′.
- Because pairing is fixed, knowing the sequence of one strand tells you the sequence of the other. In any double-stranded DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C.

In eukaryotes, most DNA is in the nucleus, wound around proteins called **histones**. Mitochondria and chloroplasts also hold small circular DNA. In prokaryotes, DNA is a single circular chromosome in the cytosol, often with small extra circles called **plasmids**.

### RNA structure and the three main types

RNA is usually **single-stranded**, contains ribose and uses uracil instead of thymine. It is generally shorter than DNA and less stable, which suits its role as a temporary working copy. The three main types are:

| Type | Role | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| **mRNA** (messenger RNA) | Carries a copy of a gene's code from DNA to a ribosome | Read in groups of three bases called codons |
| **tRNA** (transfer RNA) | Brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome | Folds into a clover-leaf shape; has an anticodon at one end and an amino acid attachment site at the 3′ end |
| **rRNA** (ribosomal RNA) | Combines with proteins to form ribosomes | Catalyses the formation of peptide bonds |

### Amino acids and peptide bonds

**Proteins** are made of one or more **polypeptides**, which are chains of **amino acids**. Each amino acid has a central carbon bonded to:

- an **amine group** (NH₂)
- a **carboxyl group** (COOH)
- a hydrogen atom
- a variable **R group** (side chain)

There are 20 amino acids commonly found in proteins, and they differ only in their R group. R groups can be non-polar, polar, or charged (acidic or basic), and these properties decide how a chain folds.

Two amino acids join by condensation: the carboxyl group of one reacts with the amine group of the next, releasing water and forming a **peptide bond**. A chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds, and making it releases n − 1 water molecules. A polypeptide has a free amine group at one end (the **N-terminus**) and a free carboxyl group at the other (the **C-terminus**).

The order of amino acids is the protein's **primary structure**. It is set by the gene, and it determines how the chain folds into its final three-dimensional shape, and therefore its function.

### The genetic code

The **genetic code** is the set of rules that link base sequences to amino acids. Its main features:

- **Triplet code**: the DNA is read in groups of three bases called **triplets**. Four bases taken three at a time give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 combinations, which is enough to code for 20 amino acids. (Pairs would give only 16, which is not enough.)
- **Codons**: the matching groups of three bases on mRNA. Of the 64 codons, 61 code for amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are **stop codons**. **AUG** is the **start codon** and also codes for methionine.
- **Anticodons**: groups of three bases on tRNA that are complementary to an mRNA codon. For example, the codon AUG pairs with the anticodon UAC.
- **Degenerate** (also called redundant): most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon. Glycine, for example, is coded by GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG. This means some changes in the third base have no effect on the protein.
- **Universal**: almost all organisms use the same codons for the same amino acids. This is strong evidence that all life shares a common ancestor, and it is why a human gene can be expressed in bacteria.
- **Non-overlapping**: each base is part of only one codon, and the code is read continuously from the start codon.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Base percentages in DNA

A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 18% adenine. What are the percentages of the other bases?

1. A pairs with T, so %T = %A = 18%.
2. A + T = 36%, so G + C = 100% − 36% = 64%.
3. G pairs with C, so %G = %C = 64% ÷ 2 = 32%.

Answer: T 18%, G 32%, C 32%. Note this only works for double-stranded DNA. In single-stranded RNA there is no rule that %A = %U.

### Example 2: From DNA triplet to anticodon

A DNA template strand contains the triplet TAC. Give the mRNA codon, the tRNA anticodon and the amino acid.

1. mRNA is complementary to the template, with U instead of T: T → A, A → U, C → G. Codon = **AUG**.
2. The anticodon is complementary to the codon: A → U, U → A, G → C. Anticodon = **UAC**.
3. Look up AUG in a codon table: **methionine** (also the start signal).

Notice the anticodon has the same bases as the DNA template triplet, but with U in place of T.

### Example 3: Building a polypeptide

A polypeptide contains 150 amino acids. How many peptide bonds does it have, and how many water molecules were released when it was made?

1. Each peptide bond joins two neighbours, so the number of bonds is one less than the number of amino acids: 150 − 1 = 149.
2. Each bond releases one water molecule by condensation, so 149 water molecules were released.
3. The minimum number of mRNA bases needed to code it is 150 × 3 = 450, plus 3 for the stop codon = 453.

## Common mistakes

- Saying RNA contains thymine, or that DNA contains ribose. Remember: DNA = deoxyribose + T; RNA = ribose + U.
- Calling the bond between nucleotides a peptide bond. Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester bonds; amino acids are joined by peptide bonds. Hydrogen bonds hold the two DNA strands together.
- Mixing up codons and anticodons. Codons are on mRNA; anticodons are on tRNA. DNA has triplets.
- Thinking degenerate means one codon codes for several amino acids. It is the other way around: several codons code for one amino acid. Each codon codes for only one thing.
- Forgetting that stop codons do not code for an amino acid, so they add no amino acid to the chain.

## Exam tips

- Use precise names: nucleotide, phosphodiester bond, peptide bond, condensation polymerisation. Vague words like 'joined' or 'stuck together' rarely earn the mark.
- When comparing DNA and RNA, give paired differences (sugar, bases, number of strands, stability, location) rather than a list of facts about one molecule.
- When explaining why the code is triplet, show the arithmetic: 4² = 16 is too few, 4³ = 64 is enough.
- Codon tables are supplied in exams. Always convert to mRNA first before using the table.

## Tips to remember

- **"Pure As Gold"**: the **pur**ines are **A**denine and **G**uanine (double ring). The pyrimidines are the rest, remembered as **"CUT the py"**: **C**ytosine, **U**racil, **T**hymine (single ring).
- **"Apple in the Tree, Car in the Garage"**: A pairs with T, C pairs with G. In RNA the apple has no tree, so A pairs with U.
- **G–C sticks harder**: G and C share three hydrogen bonds, A and T only two. Picture G–C as a three-pin plug and A–T as a two-pin plug.
- **Fence posts and rails**: in a chain of n amino acids there are n − 1 peptide bonds (like n fence posts with n − 1 rails between them), and n − 1 water molecules released by condensation.
- **Name the bond by its job** (a made-up memory trick, "P-P-H"): **P**hosphodiester bonds join nucleotides along a strand, **P**eptide bonds join amino acids, **H**ydrogen bonds hold the two DNA strands together.
- **Why triplets? Show the maths**: 4² = 16 is too few for 20 amino acids, 4³ = 64 is enough. Quick self-check: "degenerate" means many codons → one amino acid, never one codon → many.

## Key terms

- **Nucleotide** — monomer of a nucleic acid: phosphate, pentose sugar and nitrogenous base.
- **Phosphodiester bond** — bond linking the phosphate of one nucleotide to the 3′ carbon of the next nucleotide's sugar.
- **Complementary base pairing** — A pairs with T (or U in RNA) and G pairs with C.
- **Antiparallel** — the two strands of DNA run in opposite 5′ → 3′ directions.
- **Amino acid** — monomer of a protein, with an amine group, carboxyl group, hydrogen and R group on a central carbon.
- **Peptide bond** — bond between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amine group of the next.
- **Condensation polymerisation** — joining monomers into a polymer with the release of water at each bond.
- **Codon** — group of three mRNA bases that codes for one amino acid or a stop signal.
- **Anticodon** — group of three tRNA bases complementary to a codon.
- **Degenerate code** — most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
- **Universal code** — the same codons code for the same amino acids in almost all organisms.

## Summary

- DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides joined by phosphodiester bonds into a sugar-phosphate backbone.
- DNA is a double-stranded, antiparallel helix with A–T and G–C pairing; RNA is single-stranded, uses ribose and uracil, and comes as mRNA, tRNA and rRNA.
- Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; the amino acid sequence is the primary structure.
- Both nucleic acids and proteins are built by condensation polymerisation, which releases water.
- The genetic code is triplet, degenerate, universal and non-overlapping, with 61 amino acid codons, 3 stop codons and AUG as the start codon.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly lists the components of a single RNA nucleotide?
questions.explanation: An RNA nucleotide has a phosphate, the sugar ribose and one of the bases A, U, G or C, so phosphate, ribose and adenine is correct. Option A is tempting because uracil is found in RNA, but deoxyribose is the DNA sugar. Option B pairs ribose with thymine, which is only in DNA.

questions.prompt: The bond that joins two amino acids in a polypeptide is called a
questions.explanation: Amino acids are linked by peptide bonds, and each one forms by a condensation reaction that releases water. Option D names the right bond but the wrong reaction: hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds by adding water. Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides, not amino acids.

questions.prompt: Why must the genetic code be read in groups of at least three bases?

options.A: Because each amino acid contains three chemical groups that must each be coded for.
options.B: Because groups of two bases give only 16 combinations, too few to code for 20 amino acids.
options.C: Because ribosomes can only hold three bases at a time.
options.D: Because DNA has three hydrogen bonds between each base pair.

questions.explanation: With four bases, pairs give 4² = 16 combinations, which cannot cover 20 amino acids, while triplets give 4³ = 64, which is enough. Option D is tempting because of the number three, but only G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds and this has nothing to do with codon length.

questions.prompt: The codons GCU, GCC, GCA and GCG all code for alanine. This is an example of the genetic code being
questions.explanation: Several codons coding for the same amino acid is what 'degenerate' (redundant) means. Option A is a real feature of the code, but universal means the same codons are used by almost all organisms, not that several codons share one amino acid.

questions.prompt: Which statement best explains why a gene from a jellyfish can be expressed in bacteria to make the same protein?

options.A: The genetic code is universal, so the bacterial ribosomes read the codons as the same amino acids.
options.B: The genetic code is degenerate, so the bacteria can use any codon to make the protein.
options.C: Jellyfish and bacteria both contain plasmids that store the same genes.
options.D: Bacteria and jellyfish use the same sugar, deoxyribose, in their DNA.

questions.explanation: Because the code is universal, a codon such as UGG means tryptophan in both organisms, so the same amino acid sequence is built. Option B confuses degenerate with universal; degeneracy explains why some mutations are silent, not why genes work across species.

questions.prompt: A double-stranded DNA molecule contains 26% guanine. What percentage of its bases are thymine?
questions.explanation: G = C = 26%, so G + C = 52%. That leaves 48% for A + T, and since A = T, thymine is 24%. Option B (48%) is the total of A and T together, a common slip when students forget to halve it.

questions.prompt: A section of a DNA template strand reads 3′-AAG-5′. What is the anticodon of the tRNA that will pair with the matching mRNA codon?
questions.explanation: The mRNA codon is complementary to the template: 5′-UUC-3′. The anticodon is complementary and antiparallel to the codon: 3′-AAG-5′. This matches the template strand's bases (there is no T to replace here). Option D is the mRNA codon, not the anticodon, which is the most common mix-up.

questions.prompt: A protein is made of two polypeptide chains, one of 120 amino acids and one of 80 amino acids. How many water molecules were released when the peptide bonds in these two chains formed?
questions.explanation: Each chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds: 119 + 79 = 198, and each bond releases one water molecule. Option B (199) treats the two chains as one continuous chain of 200 amino acids, but the chains are separate so each loses one bond from the count.
